#### **Introduction** 

- **G** **_old has so far str

uggled at prices above $1,400. The economic and financial background points to higher prices later in the year, but sentiment is currently fragile. Good physical support is evident between $1,355 and $1,370 and the market is tight with Far Eastern premia at two-year highs. Professional investors, though, appear partly to be discounting brittle conditions in the Eurozone. January trading is likely to be choppy in narrow ranges, with some further easing possible in February after the Chinese New Year._** - **S** **_ilver traded briefly over $31 in early January but the sell-off in the sector swept it rapidly down towards $28. **I1** Independent - Informed - International Economic Indicators - January 2011 With both the dollar and the euro looking under threat from fundamental bearish pressures in the medium term, therefore, the scene is set for further investment in gold later in the year. Gold thrives on uncertainty and on headaches in the currency market. The current environment suggests that a head of steam will build up later in the year that will rekindle inflationary fears and concerns over currency volatility, both of which will argue for investment in gold as a risk hedge. For the near term, though, the investment community seems to have discounted sustained problems in Europe and this points to a period of range trading in the gold market. Strong physical demand will help to put a floor under the market but will not of itself be enough to drive prices independently higher. ##### **The Federal Reserve; more dovish than previously** The minutes of the most recent Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), released in early January, showed that two of the twelve Federal Reserve Banks (Dallas and Kansas City) had argued for a 25 basis point rise in the discount rate (i.e. the rate at which banks apply to the FOMC for ”Emergency” loans). The rate was, however, held steady at 75 basis points, effectively on the basis that the economy remained surrounded by uncertainties and that they expected growth to be “modest going forward”. Consumer spending and manufacturing activity are encouraging, but this is offset by the housing market and high unemployment. In a rare national television interview, Federal Reserve Chairman Bernanke highlighted unemployment, which has been in excess of 9% since mid-2009. He considered that it could be more than four years before unemployment returns to a “more normal unemployment rate” of approximately 5-6%. ##### **~~Precious Metals Supply-Demand Overview~~** |**~~Precious Metals Supply-Demand O~~**|**~~verview~~**|||||~~© Copyr~~|~~ight GFMS Limited~~| |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| |(tonnes)|**2004**|**2005**|**2006**|**2007**|**2008**|**2009**|**% change**

He stated that the government is not printing money, but reducing interest rates through the purchase of Treasury securities in order to stimulate economic growth. Further, the Federal Reserve is “very, very, clear” that it will “not allow inflation to rise above 2%”. In an interesting development, Fed officials seem to have taken on a more dovish tone in January. The Federal Reserve Bank Chairman of Philadelphia, for example, has softened his previously cautious stance with respect to the quantitative easing programme. It would seem that the risk of deflation is taking more of a hold in policy makers’ thinking and that any escalation in deflationary fears might well affect policy adjustments. He did, however, colour his comments with the statement that “The aggressiveness of our accommodative policy may soon backfire on us if we don’t begin to gradually reverse course”. ##### **Markets; equities now; perhaps gold again later?** The markets’ reaction to this expounding of the Fed’s philosophy has been mixed. North American investors are certainly looking to equities as a likely outperformer among the major asset classes this year, but there is still a degree of lingering concern that the fiscal stimuli of the past few months will, ultimately, lead to heightened inflationary pressures. The next FOMC meeting takes place on the 25th and 26th January; the minutes of that meeting will be released on 17th February. All in all, with the Chinese New Year of 3rd February briefly removing some buying interest (see page Au2), February looks like a volatile month for gold prices. **I3** Independent - Informed - International Economic Indicato

The Chinese market will be closed for a week for the New Year celebrations so some natural easing in physical demand in the market should be expected at that point. Chinese investors’ economic f

ears, which we outlined in our previous edition of this publication, have not abated; in fact the official CPI figure for November was 5.1% year-on-year (largely due to rapidly rising food prices) against 4.4% in October. The government’s inflation target, which had been 3%, is now 4% and local economists doubt that this will be achieved. Food inflation is generally forecast at 10% for this year. The Chinese government is under pressure to tighten liquidity, as bank lending exceeded the target last year, despite several rises in the reserve requirement. Local observers take the view that there will be excess liquidity in the Chinese market in at least the first half of this year. This, tied in with rising inflation and the government’s stated intention to battle these rising prices, are driving Chinese gold investment.
